explanations.answer: A man carrying a jug of water
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jug of water will meet you. Follow him…” and that's the whole sign. No name, no address, just a guy and a jug. I'd have asked for a second clue, friend. But verse 16 says the disciples found everything as Jesus had described.

explanations.answer: A man leading a young donkey
explanations.explanation: A donkey would be easy to spot, I'll give you that. But Jesus doesn't mention one here. He says a man carrying a jug of water will meet the two disciples, and He tells them to follow him. Only the jug made it into this sign.

explanations.answer: A woman drawing water at a well
explanations.explanation: The water part is right, so I see why this one tempts. But Jesus says a man will meet them, and he's carrying a jug of water. No well comes up in His directions. The disciples just follow the man and see which house he enters.

Jesus says the owner “…will show you a large upper room, furnished and ready.” Big, upstairs, and already set up. That's a host who thought of everything. I can't even find my own rolling pin half the time, friend.
Ooh, fancy! But Jesus never mentions a palace or a banquet hall. He says the owner “…will show you a large upper room, furnished and ready.” Big, upstairs and set up, and no red carpet needed.

A hidden inner room! Ooh, I love a secret hideout, friend. But Jesus says the owner “…will show you a large upper room, furnished and ready.” Large, upstairs, set up and waiting. Me, I once hid the last cookie so well I needed a search party to find it.
It's the other way around. Verse 16 says the disciples “…found everything as Jesus had described.” The man, the house and the room were all there. Then they prepared the Passover.
Right, it's False. Mark 14:16 says the disciples left, went into the city and found everything as Jesus had described. Then they prepared the Passover. Every detail he gave them lined up.

Jesus says, “Truly I tell you, one of you who is eating with Me will betray Me.” He says it while they're reclining and eating together. That's a hard thing to say across a dinner table. I think the room got very quiet, friend.
Jesus doesn't say anyone will take His place. He says, “…one of you who is eating with Me will betray Me.” Betray is the word, and He says it to the ones at the table.
No crowds come up here at all. Jesus is at the Passover table with the Twelve, and He says one of those eating with Him will betray Him. I think this moment belongs to the table, not to a crowd.
Mark 14:19 says they “…began to be grieved…” Then they ask Him one after another, “Surely not I?” I think grief fits, friend, when the news is about someone at your own table.
Anger makes sense on paper, but the text gives a different word. They began to be grieved, and they asked one after another, “Surely not I?” That sounds like sorrow to me, not a fight.
Fear is a fair guess, but the verse doesn't use that word. It says the disciples began to be grieved. Then they asked Him, one after another, “Surely not I?”
Jesus says the opposite. He answers, “It is one of the Twelve…” So it's someone sitting right there at the table with Him, not a stranger from outside.
Right, it's False. Jesus says, “It is one of the Twelve—the one who is dipping his hand into the bowl with Me.” So the betrayer is someone inside the circle, at that very table.

explanations.answer: Better for him if he'd never been born
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “…woe to that man by whom He is betrayed! It would be better for him if he had not been born.” I think this one is heavy, and it should be. He also says the Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him. Take that line slowly, friend.

explanations.answer: He'll be driven out of the land forever
explanations.explanation: Jesus never says anything about being driven out of a land. He says, “…woe to that man by whom He is betrayed!” and then, “It would be better for him if he had not been born.” That's a heavy line, and it's the one He gives.

explanations.answer: His name will be wiped from every record
explanations.explanation: Records and names don't come up in what Jesus says here. He says, “…woe to that man by whom He is betrayed! It would be better for him if he had not been born.” It's a sober moment, and the words are plain.
The word is body. As He hands the bread to the disciples, Jesus says, “Take it; this is My body.” They are eating together when He says it. That's a moment to hold quietly, friend.
Jesus is holding bread, and He says something about it that isn't "word." He tells the disciples, “Take it; this is My body.” He says it right as He gives the bread to them.
Gift is a nice thought, but it isn't the word Jesus uses. As He gives the bread to the disciples, He says, “Take it; this is My body.” The word is body.

Jesus says, “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.” He gives them the cup and says what it is. They all drank from it first. It's one of the most serious things He says at that table.
Harvest doesn't come up in what Jesus says. He gives the cup to them, they all drink, and He says, “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.” That's the name He gives it.
The meal is a feast, so I see where that came from. But Jesus doesn't call the cup a sign. He says, “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.”

Jesus says, “…I will no longer drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it anew in the kingdom of God.” Notice the word anew. He's talking about a day still ahead. That's the kind of line that keeps my ovens warm and ready, friend.
The temple courts aren't mentioned here. Jesus says He will drink it anew “…in the kingdom of God.” He's pointing to a day still ahead, and He doesn't name a date.
Jerusalem sounds natural, but Jesus names a different place. He says, “…until that day when I drink it anew in the kingdom of God.” The kingdom of God is where He points.

On the Mount of Olives, Jesus tells them, “You will all fall away…” He points to what is written: “I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.” It's a hard thing to hear from Him. And the word is all, not some.
That would be the happy ending, but Jesus says the opposite. He tells them, “You will all fall away…” He doesn't soften it. The all in that line is plain.

explanations.answer: They will all preach in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Nobody is sent off to preach anywhere in this moment. Jesus says, “You will all fall away…” and quotes what is written about the sheep being scattered. I think that's a hard word to hear on the Mount of Olives.
Jesus says, “But after I have risen…” Right after the hard news about the scattering, He says what comes after. That one little word gives the whole line its hope, friend.
Jesus says, “…I will go ahead of you into Galilee.” He doesn't just say He'll come back. He says He goes ahead of them. That's a promise with a destination.
Returned is close in feel, but it isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, “But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.” The word is risen.

Bethany is a real place, baker, so I get why it popped up. But Jesus says, “…I will go ahead of you into Galilee.” Picking the wrong town is like showing up at the wrong house with a full tray of cookies, big smile, knocking away, and nobody's expecting you. The place is Galilee.
Jerusalem is a big name, so I see why it came to mind. But Jesus names a different place. He says, “…I will go ahead of you into Galilee.”

Jesus tells Peter, one of the Twelve, “this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” That's both the number and the timing, and Jesus doesn't leave it vague. Peter has just said he never will. Ouch, friend.
Hiding isn't what Jesus says. He tells Peter, one of the Twelve, “this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” The word is deny.

Bethany doesn't come up in what Jesus says to Peter, one of the Twelve. He tells him, “this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” It's about what Peter will say, not where he'll go.
Peter does the opposite. Mark 14:31 says he “kept insisting.” He doubles down with, “Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You.” No backing up at all.
Right, it's False. Peter kept insisting, “Even if I have to die with You, I will never deny You.” He says it after Jesus has just told him what will happen. He was holding his ground, friend.
The text says otherwise. After Peter's promise, it adds, “And all the others said the same thing.” So Peter isn't the only voice on the Mount of Olives. The whole group is promising.
Right, it's False. Mark 14:31 says, “And all the others said the same thing.” So Peter isn't alone in what he says. The other disciples say it right along with him.
